title: WHEN MONEY BECOMES A PERMISSION SYSTEM
subtitle: PRIVACY. CENSORSHIP. CONTROL. THEY ARE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS.

blocks.text: THREE QUESTIONS: WHO CAN SEE? WHO CAN STOP? WHO HOLDS THE KEYS? THEY ARE NOT THE SAME QUESTION.
CRYPTO OFTEN COLLAPSES THREE IDEAS INTO ONE.

Privacy, censorship resistance and self-custody are regularly spoken about as though possessing one automatically gives you the others. It does not. They describe different properties of a financial system.

Understanding the difference matters because a payment can be self-custodied yet public, private yet dependent on an intermediary, or difficult to censor while still exposing a detailed transaction history.
01 // PRIVACY — WHO CAN SEE?

Privacy concerns information. Who can observe the sender, recipient, amount, balance or transaction graph? Bitcoin demonstrates the distinction clearly: a user can control private keys directly while transactions remain public and permanently stored on the network. Self-custody does not automatically hide activity.
02 // CENSORSHIP RESISTANCE — WHO CAN STOP?

Censorship resistance concerns the ability to get a valid transaction accepted despite an intermediary or participant preferring that it not happen. Decentralized networks can reduce reliance on a single gatekeeper, but censorship resistance is not binary. Network topology, block production, fees, policy, custodians and access points can all affect the practical path from signing a transaction to settlement.
03 // SELF-CUSTODY — WHO HOLDS THE KEYS?

Self-custody concerns control over the credentials required to spend. If you hold the relevant private keys, you do not need an exchange to sign a transaction for you. If a custodian holds them, your balance may economically belong to you while the custodian controls the actual signing authority and can impose withdrawal policies.
OWNING THE KEYS ANSWERS WHO CAN AUTHORIZE A SPEND. IT DOES NOT ANSWER WHO CAN OBSERVE IT.
04 // ONE SYSTEM CAN SCORE DIFFERENTLY ON EACH PROPERTY

Physical cash can provide strong local transaction privacy and direct possession, yet moving it over distance requires physical transport or an intermediary. A bank account can offer confidentiality from the general public while remaining visible to the institution and subject to its controls and legal obligations. Transparent cryptocurrency can provide self-custody and decentralized settlement while publishing transaction history. Shielded cryptocurrency can add cryptographic protection for payment details while preserving independent verification.

None of these descriptions means every implementation provides perfect privacy, perfect control or perfect resistance to censorship. Architecture determines which parties must be trusted and which information must be revealed.
05 // PERMISSION CAN APPEAR AT THE EDGES

Even a permissionless base protocol can meet permissioned infrastructure. Exchanges can control deposits and withdrawals. Hosted wallets can control keys. Payment processors can decide what they support. Internet access and network observation create another layer. The properties of the base ledger and the properties of the surrounding ecosystem should not be confused.
06 // PRIVACY CAN EXIST WITHOUT HIDING THE RULES

Zero-knowledge proofs introduce an important architectural separation. The rules can remain public and independently verifiable while selected transaction details remain private. Verification does not have to mean publishing every fact used to satisfy the rules.
A SYSTEM CAN PROVE THAT THE RULES WERE FOLLOWED WITHOUT TURNING EVERY PAYMENT INTO PUBLIC PROPERTY.
THE BETTER QUESTION

Instead of asking whether a form of money is simply free, private or decentralized, ask narrower questions. Who controls the keys? Who can observe the transaction? Who can refuse service? Who validates settlement? What information becomes permanent? What happens when the system touches a custodian?
Those answers reveal the architecture without requiring slogans.
OWNING THE KEYS ANSWERS WHO CAN SPEND. PRIVACY ANSWERS WHO GETS TO WATCH.
